items.rule: A nonessential phrase set off by an opening comma must be closed by a comma before the main verb.
items.passage: The report on the city's water quality, which had been commissioned after several complaints from residents ______ that lead levels had fallen sharply since 2019.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choice_notes: semicolons cannot separate a subject from its verb
a colon cannot separate a subject from its verb
items.explanation: The phrase 'which had been commissioned after several complaints from residents' is nonessential, so it must be enclosed by commas on both sides. Only the first choice supplies the closing comma before the main verb 'concluded'. A semicolon or colon between a subject and its verb is never correct.
items.skill_note: Check that both sides of a nonessential phrase are closed.

items.rule: Its is possessive; it's means it is.
items.passage: The company announced ______ new headquarters would open in the spring, nearly a year later than planned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choice_notes: expands to 'it is', which does not fit
no apostrophe is used for a possessive pronoun
expands to 'it is', which does not fit
items.explanation: The sentence needs a possessive pronoun modifying 'headquarters': 'its'. 'It's' and 'it is' would each mean 'it is new headquarters', and possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, so 'its'' is not a word.
items.skill_note: Test the expansion: if 'it is' fits, use it's; otherwise use its.

items.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with a noun inside a prepositional phrase.
items.passage: The collection of letters and photographs donated by three generations of the family ______ now housed in the county archive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choice_notes: agrees with 'letters and photographs' instead of 'collection'
items.explanation: The subject is 'The collection', which is singular; 'of letters and photographs donated by three generations of the family' only modifies it. The singular present 'is' is the only choice that agrees.
items.skill_note: Cross out every prepositional phrase between subject and verb, then check agreement.

items.rule: Items joined by 'and' in a series must share the same grammatical form.
items.passage: The internship teaches students how to draft a budget, how to present findings to a client, and ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choice_notes: breaks the pattern of 'how to' plus verb
a noun phrase where the other items are verb phrases
items.explanation: The first two items are 'how to draft' and 'how to present', so the third must also be 'how to' plus a verb: 'how to negotiate a deadline'. Parallel structure in a list is decided by the form of the first item.
items.skill_note: Match the third item to the first, not to the one nearest it.

items.rule: An introductory participial phrase must modify the subject of the main clause.
items.passage: Walking through the exhibition for the first time, ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the visitors were struck by the size of the canvases
the size of the canvases struck the visitors
the canvases' size was striking to visitors
it struck the visitors how large the canvases were
choice_notes: the size did not walk through the exhibition
the canvases' size did not walk through the exhibition
an expletive subject leaves the modifier unattached
items.explanation: 'Walking through the exhibition' must describe whoever is doing the walking. Only the first choice makes 'the visitors' the subject, so only it attaches the modifier correctly.
items.skill_note: Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase, then make that the subject.

items.rule: Use the past perfect for an action completed before another past action.
items.passage: By the time the survey was published in 1998, the volunteers ______ more than two thousand hours of observations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choice_notes: present perfect does not fit a completed past sequence
present tense contradicts the past frame
items.explanation: The logging happened before the 1998 publication, and both events are in the past, so the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'had logged'.
items.skill_note: Two past actions in sequence: the earlier one gets 'had'.

items.passage: The committee kept a [reserve] of funds for unexpected repairs, refusing to spend the money even when other departments asked for it.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "reserve" most nearly mean?
choices: money set aside for future need
an athlete held back as a substitute
choice_notes: a different sense of reserve, not one about money
items.explanation: The text is about funds kept for unexpected repairs, so 'reserve' means money set aside. The other choices are real senses of the word, but none fits a sentence about a committee holding funds.
items.skill_note: Cover the choices and define the word in your own words first.

items.passage: The director's [charged] remarks left the room silent; no one had expected the meeting to turn so quickly.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "charged" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a legal sense that does not fit remarks
items.explanation: The remarks silenced a room and changed the mood of a meeting, so 'charged' describes emotional intensity. The other choices are literal senses of the same word.
items.skill_note: Context clues ('left the room silent') decide which sense applies.

items.passage: The team's [novel] approach to filtering water used gravity and sand rather than electricity, which made it usable in places with no power grid.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "novel" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: the noun sense, not the adjective
items.explanation: Here 'novel' is an adjective modifying 'approach', and the sentence emphasises that the method avoided electricity, so it means new and original.
items.skill_note: Check the word's part of speech in the sentence before choosing a meaning.

items.passage: The instrument's [fine] adjustments took nearly an hour, each one measured in fractions of a millimetre.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "fine" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a quality judgement, not a measurement sense
items.explanation: The phrase 'measured in fractions of a millimetre' tells you 'fine' refers to small, precise adjustments rather than to quality.
items.skill_note: The words after the target often define it more precisely than the sentence's tone.

items.passage: The design's [economy] came from using a single part to perform three separate jobs, which cut both cost and weight.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "economy" most nearly mean?
choices: a country's system of trade and finance
the cheapest class of air travel
choice_notes: too narrow: the text is about arrangement, not price alone
items.explanation: 'Economy' here names the efficiency achieved by making one part do three jobs. That arrangement cut cost and weight, but the word describes the efficiency rather than a price reduction.
items.skill_note: When two choices are close, pick the one that matches what the sentence emphasises.

items.passage: The first trials produced almost no usable data. ______, the team continued refining the instrument for another year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: signals a result, but the second sentence resists the first
introduces an example, not a contrast
items.explanation: The second sentence describes continuing despite failure, which is a contrast: 'Nevertheless'. 'Therefore' would reverse the logic, and the other two signal example and similarity.
items.skill_note: Name the relationship in your own words ('but' or 'so') before you look at the choices.

items.passage: The soil in the valley drains unusually quickly. ______, farmers there plant drought-tolerant varieties rather than thirsty ones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: signals contrast where there is a result
items.explanation: Fast-draining soil causes farmers to choose drought-tolerant crops, so the second sentence is a consequence: 'Consequently'.
items.skill_note: Ask 'does sentence two happen because of sentence one?'

items.passage: The archive preserves the town's letters, ledgers, and maps. ______, it holds a nearly complete run of the local newspaper from 1881 to 1974.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence adds another category of material the archive holds, so the transition must signal addition: 'Moreover'.
items.skill_note: Two lists of the same kind take an addition transition.

items.passage: The method is expensive and slow, and no one expects it to become cheaper soon. ______, it remains the only technique that works at this scale.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: signals a result, but the second sentence concedes rather than follows
items.explanation: The sentence concedes the drawbacks and then asserts a countervailing fact, which is the concession relationship 'Even so'. 'Therefore' would claim the drawbacks cause the usefulness.
items.skill_note: A 'despite that' relationship takes Even so / Nevertheless / That said.

items.passage: Coral reefs build their structure from calcium carbonate, which the polyps secrete slowly over decades. When seawater warms, the algae living inside the polyps abandon them and the coral loses its colour, a process called bleaching. Bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but if the algae do not return within a few weeks the polyps starve and the reef begins to erode. Some researchers now argue that the more useful measure of a reef's health is not its colour but the rate at which it is building new carbonate.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Colour is an unreliable indicator of a reef's condition, and the rate of carbonate accretion is a better one.
Bleaching inevitably kills coral and destroys the reef within weeks.
Algae are the organisms primarily responsible for building reef structure.
Warming oceans are the only threat to the survival of coral reefs.
choice_notes: contradicts the text: polyps secrete the carbonate
too broad; the text never claims it is the only threat
items.explanation: The passage moves from how reefs are built, through what bleaching does and does not mean, to the researchers' claim that accretion rate beats colour as a health measure. That final claim is the point of the whole passage.
items.skill_note: The main idea is usually in the last sentence when the passage walks toward a conclusion.

items.passage: Coral reefs build their structure from calcium carbonate, which the polyps secrete slowly over decades. When seawater warms, the algae living inside the polyps abandon them and the coral loses its colour, a process called bleaching. [Bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but if the algae do not return within a few weeks the polyps starve and the reef begins to erode.] Some researchers now argue that the more useful measure of a reef's health is not its colour but the rate at which it is building new carbonate.
items.stem: The sentence in brackets primarily serves to
choices: qualify a possible misunderstanding by distinguishing bleaching from death while noting the real risk
provide evidence that bleaching always leads to the collapse of a reef
describe the chemical process by which polyps secrete calcium carbonate
introduce the researchers' view that colour should be the primary measure of health
choice_notes: overstates: the text says the coral is 'not necessarily dead'
the text argues the opposite at the end
items.explanation: The sentence corrects an assumption ('not necessarily dead') and then names the actual danger (starvation and erosion). That is a qualification, not evidence for the stronger claim in the second choice.
items.skill_note: Ask what the sentence does to the argument, not what it says.

items.passage: Carnegie funded more than 2,500 libraries, but he rarely chose their books. The design was standardised: a small reading room, a closed stack, and a librarian's desk positioned to see the door. What varied was the collection, assembled locally by women's clubs and school boards. Historians who study these buildings now argue that the standardised architecture mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the historians mentioned in the text believe that
choices: whether a town obtained a library depended more on local organisers than on the standardised building plan
Carnegie's architects designed each library to suit the town that received it
the size of a library's collection was determined by its building's design
women's clubs and school boards preferred standardised buildings to varied ones
choice_notes: contradicted by 'what varied was the collection'
never claimed; their role was assembling collections
items.explanation: The historians argue the architecture 'mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all' — so local organising, not the plan, determined who got a library.
items.skill_note: Inference answers are paraphrases of a causal claim already in the text.

items.passage: Carnegie funded more than 2,500 libraries, but he rarely chose their books. The design was standardised: a small reading room, a closed stack, and a librarian's desk positioned to see the door. What varied was the collection, assembled locally by women's clubs and school boards. Historians who study these buildings now argue that the standardised architecture mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all.
items.stem: According to the text, what varied from one Carnegie library to another?
choices: the design of the reading room
the position of the librarian's desk
choice_notes: the text says the design was standardised
the desk position is named as part of the standard plan
items.explanation: 'What varied was the collection' is stated directly. The reading room and the librarian's desk are listed as parts of the standardised design.
items.skill_note: Detail questions are literal — find the sentence and match it exactly.

items.passage: Widening a road rarely reduces congestion for long. New capacity attracts drivers who previously took transit or travelled at other hours, and within a few years traffic volumes rise to fill the space that was added.
items.passage2: The evidence on induced demand is strong, but it describes regional networks rather than single streets. A city that removes a lane from one street may see traffic vanish from that street without worsening congestion elsewhere, because drivers disperse across the grid.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim made in Text 1?
choices: By accepting that added capacity attracts traffic while limiting that conclusion to networks rather than individual streets
By rejecting the evidence on induced demand as unsound in every case
By arguing that removing a lane always worsens congestion on nearby streets
By claiming that drivers never change their routes in response to new capacity
choice_notes: Text 2 says traffic may vanish from that street
both texts assume drivers respond to capacity
items.explanation: Text 2 grants that 'the evidence on induced demand is strong' and then restricts its scope to regional networks rather than single streets. That is agreement plus a qualification.
items.skill_note: Cross-text answers usually combine agreement on one point with a limit on another.
